Freezing temperatures and unsettled conditions could sweep the UK as the El Niño weather phenomenon continues to wreak havoc on global weather.
Experts are predicting a wet and stormy autumn that could develop into an icy winter after the “super El Niño” smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest event in history.
The Met Office said the “unprecedented” phenomenon, which has already helped push temperatures to reach the hottest summer on record, will continue to have “far-reaching” implications for weather conditions across the world.





El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It takes place when sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern Pacific become significantly warmer than average, altering atmospheric circulation patterns and influencing weather around the globe.

The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño. 


“Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide.” 
Forecasters warned the phenomenon could disrupt a large, high-altitude ring of swirling cold winds spinning above the Arctic known as the stratospheric polar vortex. He calculated that for a homeowner borrowing £250,000 over 25 years on a two-year fixed rate a household could reduce repayments by roughly £29 per month, which amounts to just under £700 in just two years.  
An energy efficient home can not only reduce your mortgage payments and your bills – it also increases the value of your property. Rightmove’s Greener Homes Report found that moving from an EPC rating of D to C could add around 3 per cent to a home’s value. With an average house price in the UK of around £300,000, that amounts to £9,000.

articles.title: Strategy will safeguard nature for generations
articles.raw_rss: Local Nature Recovery Strategy is approved for one of England's "most nature-depleted areas".
articles.raw_meta: Local Nature Recovery Strategy is approved for one of England's "most nature-depleted areas".
articles.jina_text:
More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come". 
West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.
It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".
Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.
A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges. 
"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."
Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."
He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."
Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

“Gospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of central Croatia.
Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried.

In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site.
“I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says.


View image in fullscreen
An illegal waste site in Gospić in August. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
The waste became a blight on the community and a recent report from the Croatian Institute of Public Health revealed Pfas “forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil.


Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have been linked to serious health conditions, including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment.
Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water.
“I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.”


View image in fullscreen
Residents took to filming lorries going in and out of one of the dumping sites on the outskirts of Gospić, seen here last month. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
In February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste.
The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets by Europol and were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity.


Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference.
Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there.

Convicted terrorist Abu Hamza’s family home is receiving a £70,000 facelift, paid for by British taxpayers.







The £1.7 million Edwardian home, based in a conservation area of Shepherd’s Bush, will see new windows and doors installed, as well as solar panels and loft insulation.




Hamza’s wife, Najat Chaffe, is the only person registered at the five-bedroom council house - with the hate cleric serving a life sentence in a US jail.

Ms Chaffe’s “tenancy for life” deal means that the Labour-run Hammersmith and Fulham Council cannot kick her out, and have an obligation to maintain it.




She moved into the house in 1995, claiming they had separated, and Hamza’s eight children were raised in the property.




Three of his sons have since served jail sentences for offences related to drugs, money laundering and fraud.


Radical cleric Abu Hamza





Hamza, the hook-handed former imam of Finsbury Park Mosque, never officially lived at the address but was seen there on a number of occasions before his first arrest in 2004.











Hamza, 68, was jailed in the UK in 2006 for inciting racial hatred and soliciting murder.




He was extradited to the US in 2014 for plotting the kidnap of 16 tourists in Yemen, which resulted in the deaths of four hostages.




He was sentenced to life without parole by a New York court, and is currently in a maximum-security prison in Colorado.











Hammersmith and Fulham council’s Conservative opposition leader Jose Afonso said: “This is a disgusting waste of public money.




“Residents will be appalled to know that not only are we housing the families of terrorists, we are doing so in five-bedroom houses and paying for extensive upgrades.”








The council said it was bound by law to upgrade around 1,000 properties.




Planning permission has been submitted, but not yet approved, for works due for completion before the end of the decade.

How hot will it get in your nearest city tomorrow? How quickly will the planet’s ice melt and its corals die off? How many huge, costly climate disasters will hit this year? If you’re inclined to do so, you can now place online bets on how the weather and the broader, longer-term climate crisis will play out.
In the US, big online prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are considering a new area of growth beyond mere sport and crypto: the climate itself. Kalshi recently reported 500% growth in weather and climate wagers over the past year, taking the market to a $1.1bn, and is now partnering with the Weather Company, which owns the Weather Channel, to boost its credibility in this new arena.

What does this mean for our ability to predict the future of our climate? More, after this week’s most important reads.

View image in fullscreen
Large bets, which are now banned, were placed on Kalshi and Polymarket during the Los Angeles fires in 2025. Photograph: Agustin Paullier/AFP/Getty Images
Betting on the weather isn’t new, but some climate scientists have been left feeling queasy about people placing bets on the well-documented breakdown of a stable climate, caused by the burning of fossil fuels.


Such bets, they argue, trivialise and gamify raw human suffering, distancing people rather than rallying them to act on the climate crisis. Particular alarm has been raised about the consequences of betting on wildfires, after large wagers were placed on the Los Angeles fires last year (Kalshi and Polymarket stress they have banned such betting, due to unintended incentives for would-be arsonists).
“I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” said Kaitlyn Trudeau, a scientist at the non-profit Climate Central. Trudeau’s own grandfather lost his home in the LA fires, and she was aghast to find that people had been betting on the disaster.
“I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides,” she said. “They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.”
When I covered the story this month, though, it was striking to me how these prediction markets, which are essentially a gauge of public opinion, see their role as forecasting events in the natural world. Good morning. Here we are, stumbling into an oddly warm autumn and with the aftermath of a ceaselessly dry summer all around us in our parched parks and fire-ravaged forests.
With the change in season, the headlines are no less gruelling. At the start of the week, more than 450,000 people are predicted to die from an unprecedented El Niño over the next six months. At the end of the week, a report by UK intelligence chiefs reveals the extent to which the collapse of natural systems threatens security and defence around the world – a report which, as the Guardian revealed, was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer’s leadership. Meanwhile, as Hettie has written about in a previous newsletter, right-leaning climate sceptics continue to seed doubt about the glaring reality wherever they may.



Overload, silencing and misinformation can generate fear, suspicion, grief, helplessness, a compulsion to look away or to focus on paying the next bill. But this summer, I’ve been hearing about another climate briefing – in film form – that aims to engage all of those emotions. It’s as much about giving people the information they deserve as it is about helping them deal with it once they have it.
You won’t see it on Netflix, but your neighbour might be screening it at the local scout hall this weekend: for today’s newsletter, I spoke to Nick Oldridge, co-founder of the People’s Emergency Briefing, about how a film about the end of the world became a grassroots movement. First, the headlines.
Five big stories
 
 
UN general assembly | Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza. 
 
UK news | Far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy while a rescuer was onboard. 
 
Iran | Iran says it has told Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some frozen assets. 
 
Ukraine | Ukrainian refugees fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments. 
 
World news | Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over AI, trade and Taiwan.

The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves.
But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area.



  
 
 
 
 
 
🏠🌤️ How was summer 2026 near you? 
A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. 
As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below.  
Data up to August 2026   
☀️ Temperature 
In the UK summer temperatures have been above average. 
The maximum daily temperature was 21.3C on average, which is 2.4C above what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Virtually all of the UK experienced above average temperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. 
Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland. 
 
    
Average daily maximum in summer 2026 compared with the 1991-2020 average  
 
Average daily maximum temperature map key 
 
Colder: blue 
Warmer: red  
 
 
-4C: deepest blue 
No Change: white 
+4C: deepest red       
🌧️ Rainfall 
Rainfall in the UK has been below average this summer. 
Across the country a total of 195mm of rain fell on average, which is 23% below what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. 
 
    
Total rainfall in summer 2026 as a percentage of 1991-2020 average summer rainfall  
 
Total rainfall map key 
 
Drier: brown 
Wetter: blue  
 
 
-100%: deepest brown 
No Change: white 
+100%: deepest blue          
About the data  
 
Where does the data come from? 
This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset     (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. 
The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. 
The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

A rare wildflower may have been wiped out in southern England after a summer of record heat and drought, conservationists have warned.




The field gentian, once widespread across Britain, was until recently so abundant in the New Forest in Hampshire that conservationists said counting the flowers was a challenge.








But after 2026 brought record warmth, successive heatwaves and severe drought — the third extreme summer in just five years — the plant may have disappeared from southern England altogether.




Experts described its possible disappearance as a “canary in the mine” for climate-driven species loss.




The Species Recovery Trust, a charity working to save some of Britain’s most endangered species, said the potential loss was “deeply worrying” because the field gentian had previously been abundant wherever it grew.


Dry and barren land in southern England following the summer's record-breaking heatwaves
The Species Recovery Trust/PA Wire




Dominic Price, director of the Species Recovery Trust, said the plant’s habitat — dry, “skeletal” grassland — was on the “absolute front line” of climate change.













“These habitats are becoming parched and dead in hot, dry weather,” he said.




The field gentian’s disappearance would be a striking example of how increasingly frequent heat and drought can push even locally abundant species towards extinction.




In 2022, when temperatures in the UK soared to 40C for the first time on record amid an extremely hot, dry summer, field gentian populations crashed for the first time across all known sites in the south of England, and went extinct at a county-level in Devon.









Populations recovered slightly the following year, and it was thought the New Forest populations could survive, due to their sheer size – often more than 5,000 plants at each site – and their ability for seeds to move with livestock into more sheltered areas.




But then populations were hit by successive record hot summers and droughts, in 2025 and again this year.


Field gentians growing in southern England
The Species Recovery Trust/PA Wire




The Species Recovery Trust has confirmed it has been unable to locate a single field gentian plant in the New Forest for the second year in a row.

The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination

Editorial





Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice





Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.
The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.



While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them is likely to be on food supplies.


View image in fullscreen
Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty

Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. Senators’ report says taxpayers face higher bills after ‘bargain’ between president and major polluters




The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade after responding to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, leaving American taxpayers to shoulder higher bills and public health costs associated with pollution, according to a new report.
Released on Thursday by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, the report details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration.

The senators said: “The Trump administration has delivered right back, handing polluters benefits worth hundreds of billions of dollars. The estimate of $190bn savings for industry is calculated from existing tax breaks and subsidies over the next 10 years plus new benefits delivered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to an analysis by Senator Bernie Sanders for legislation he proposed with Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to eliminate “handouts” for industry.

An oil spill stretching for around 2km has closed the M61 southbound in Greater Manchester, with motorists facing three miles of congestion and delays.
A National Highways spokesperson said two separate incidents took place on the M61 southbound on Thursday morning - a "significant" oil spillage from an HGV and a car fire. They clarified that the oil spill led to the closure of the carriageway between junction four (Watergate Lane Interchange) and junction two (Worsley Braided Interchange).
National Highways said oil spread across lanes one and two for approximately 2km (1.2 miles) as the HGV travelled along the motorway at around 8.20am. The carriageway was closed to allow a clean-up operation to take place safely.
National Highways said traffic officers are managing traffic at the scene and warned of delays of up to 35 minutes.
Separately, fire crews attended a car fire on the M61 southbound between junction five (Hunger Hill Interchange) and junction four (Watergate Lane Interchange) shortly after 9.30am, Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service said. The vehicle was moved to the hard shoulder, and crews remained at the scene for around 20 minutes. No injuries were reported.

articles.jina_text:
Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.


View image in fullscreen
The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, visiting the Vantara zoo in Gujarat in March 2025. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

It was a stifling evening in July and Matt Phelps was out for a stroll, when a piercing, whirring noise stopped him in his tracks. As an ecologist, Phelps knows his fauna – and he could think of no UK creature that could emit such a sound.
“It was like the classic sound effect of a cricket in a film, a beeping sort of little trilling sound,” said Phelps, who works at Knepp Estate in West Sussex. He returned with entomologist Graeme Lyons to track it down. But the sound, though incredibly loud, “seemed to be all around us … it was very ventriloquial”.

The duo hunted for three hours. Night fell before they realised their quarry was, said Phelps, “literally below the ground where we stood”.


View image in fullscreen
A female Verge cricket. Photograph: Frederic Grimaitre/Alamy
Sure enough, in a crack in the parched clay they made the first identification of a Verge (or Bordeaux) cricket (Eumodicogryllus bordigalensis) in the British Isles.


Once they announced it, other reports poured in. “It turns out there’s been this wave of them right at the moment when there was an enormous wildfire in Bordeaux,” said Phelps. “And it made you think: have some of these things fled the flames of southern Europe?”
Verge crickets are just one of many “first sightings” of insects on the UK mainland this summer. It’s been an “extraordinary flood”, he said. And it’s not just the professionals who are finding them.
Jackie Harmer, a retired secretary from North Cheshire, was one week into her new hobby of moth-trapping when she found an odd-looking creature native to the Iberian peninsula, Odice pergrata – a first for the UK.
And David Cousins, a city trader who collects moths by night at his home in north Essex, opened his box one June dawn to find a white moth with bluish markings.

Two decades after the release of his groundbreaking documentary An Inconvenient Truth, Al Gore has admitted he was surprised by the ferocious, ongoing backlash from the fossil fuel industry and its political allies. But the former US vice-president insists he still has optimism the world will confront the climate crisis.

Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutrality




Europe’s biggest economy, Germany, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045, despite fierce debate about its green policies.
In a roadmap published on Wednesday, the German government set out for the first time an explicit promise of “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. Previous pledges were only for “carbon neutrality”.

The plans include ramping up renewable energy from 55% to 80% of electricity generation by 2030, with an additional 12GW of onshore wind, and a target of 215GW of solar energy by 2030. The previously stated target of winding down coal use in the next decade, with a view to an exit from coal in 2038, was also reaffirmed, with the potential for an earlier target of 2035.
Emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, will be cut by 30% by 2030, in accordance with a global methane pledge signed in 2021.


Andreas Sieber, head of global political strategy at 350.org, said the plan marked a “notable shift” in making the phaseout of fossil fuels an explicit policy goal. But he warned that Germany’s ministry for economic affairs and energy was also pushing intensely for greater use of gas.
“The economic ministry keeps sabotaging the transition away from fossil fuels,” he said. “This year has shown in the starkest terms that fossil-fuel dependence is a risk for everyone as it exposes households and businesses in Germany and around the world to price shocks, volatility and geopolitical insecurity.”
Germany’s former climate envoy Jennifer Morgan said the government must put more effort into electrifying transport and heating. “Accelerating the shift from coal, oil and gas to clean renewables will bolster energy independence and insulate consumers from price shocks at a critical moment,” she said. “However, a roadmap is only the starting line.”
She said the strategy must be paired with a faster, more deliberate rollout of green electrification.
The push for heat pumps to replace gas boilers came under attack from the far-right wing of German politics after a heating law was passed in 2023 that would have banned the installation of most oil and gas heating. Alternative für Deutschland made the issue a key campaigning point and forced a watering down of the rules earlier this year, while the party’s co-leader Alice Weidel has described wind turbines as “windmills of shame”. Heat pumps now make up about half of all new domestic heating systems.

Britain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, the environment secretary is to announce in New York.
The announcement on Wednesday will come as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings this year’s “supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally.

Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain after threats by the US administration this year to dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations.
In June, the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced an international alliance with Canada as part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations.


In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections.
Angela Eagle will announce the UK is to join the scheme at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, at the UN headquarters in New York.
Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before.
The environment secretary will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.”
“Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. The “super” El Nino weather event and the record global heat it is driving could cause almost half a million additional deaths worldwide over the next six months, a new report has warned.
Researchers say that up to 451,000 extra heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be linked to El Nino, compared with the number of heat deaths expected in a typical year.

At Climate Week, Elmo recalls a storm on Sesame Street: ‘Courage is when you still help others’


New York event hears about the red Muppet’s fears during a recent storm as climate crisis increasingly affects children




A generation of political leaders has failed to galvanize sufficient action on the climate crisis for so long now that it was perhaps little surprise that an audience in New York City turned to a three-and-a-half-year-old red furry monster for inspiration on Tuesday.
Elmo, the Sesame Street denizen, made a starry appearance at a Climate Week event that highlighted how the impacts of global heating affect children. The red creature, who frequently refers to himself in the third person, recounted to the audience his fear when a storm hit Sesame Street, an event depicted in a recent episode that featured the singer Post Malone.

“We all feel scared sometimes, but courage is when you feel scared but you still help others,” Elmo said at the event, which was named “Big Storms, Big Feelings”. “I tried to help others by giving lots of hugs and playing music on Elmo’s xylophone. When the storm passed Sesame Street didn’t look like Sesame Street, there was trash and branches all over the place.”
Elmo revealed that, much like a prepper, he had a “go bag” ready for the disaster and that the residents of Sesame Street banded together to help their neighborhood clean up after the storm. “Home is the people who make the place special,” he added. “So long as you’re with the people you love, you’ll be home. And that’s true in any weather.”

A young boy watches dark storm clouds from a bedroom window as severe weather affects the midwest in Monroe, Wisconsin, on 14 April. Photograph: Ross Harried/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
These sentiments were warmly received by the New York audience, who had clearly moved on from Elmo’s ambiguous support of the New York Knicks in last season’s NBA basketball playoff finals.


While media and political focus on the climate crisis has waned, despite a cavalcade of recent disasters, a Sesame Street executive at the event said the show is looking to find avenues for children to talk about the issue.
Kim Foulds, the vice-president of research and insight at Sesame Workshop, said a study was taken to “understand how children make sense of extreme weather and how their parents navigate those events across a global, diverse context”.

There is hope in solar power. As the UN meets, we are urging leaders to pursue a clear goal: clean energy for all by 2030 
 
 
Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end 





As climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad.
Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum.

The host superpower is attacking country after country in search of oily “energy dominance”; even the noblest of its opponents (Canada’s Mark Carney, hope of democratic rebirth in the Americas) is busy building new oil and gas pipelines in the hopes it can bolster his besieged economy. Britain, which finally purged coal power from its energy system last year, now seems poised to start new drilling in the North Sea. If there’s an apocalyptic fear that can still rouse politicians to action, it seems to be AI agents breaking through firewalls, not European nations facing firestorms.


But there is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy.

From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together.

We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels.
Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.

Small island nations have urged world leaders gathered in New York not to abandon efforts to limit global warming to 1.5C, warning that the goal remains a legal obligation rather than an aspiration.
The Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), a coalition of 39 small islands and low-lying coastal nations, said in a statement delivered at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that "1.5°C is not an arbitrary goal that would be nice to achieve. It is the legally affirmed limit, endorsed by the UNGA, committed to by countries to protect people, ecosystems and economies".
The statement, delivered by Anne Rasmussen, Aosis's lead climate change negotiator, said the best available science showed that limiting the scale and duration of any overshoot of 1.5°C, and bringing warming back under that threshold, remained possible. 





"We absolutely cannot surrender our pursuit of 1.5°C," it said.
Ms Rasmussen said countries gathered for the assembly's 81st session needed to "treat escalating climate change impacts with the urgency this crisis merits", adding that "clear, concrete commitments must be set out to effectively respond to climate change and realign with 1.5°C."

articles.raw_rss: The 'Godzilla' El Niño is projected to cause more than 450,000 heat-related deaths in the next six months
articles.raw_content:
Nearly half a million people are projected to die in the next six months from soaring temperatures brought by the super El Niño, which has already reached record-breaking levels.



The climate phenomenon, which forms in the Pacific Ocean, is “firmly established and is expected to strengthen further” in the coming months before peaking at the end of the year, according to the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO).



Climate scientists now predict 451,000 people across the world will die due to additional heat. 



Professor Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab which produced the report on additional deaths, said this is “such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives”.



The temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean where the El Niño forms has now reached 3.08°C, latest data shows. This is above the 3.02°C registered in November 2015 – the previous high in 150 years of records. The temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.





El Niño is part of a natural cycle, called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, and forms when warmer waters spread across the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. It is associated with widespread changes in the climate system that can last for up to a year.



The WMO said there was an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 per cent” that this El Niño will last until February 2027.

Fears are mounting that the next UN secretary general will downgrade the priority of the climate crisis, according to climate and civil society experts.
The current secretary general, António Guterres, has been the most forthright on the subject, calling fossil fuel companies “the godfathers of climate chaos” and warning governments they are rushing down a “highway to hell” by failing to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

His repeated championing of the urgency of the crisis and willingness to take on vested interests are credited with significant global impacts, forcing governments to confront their policy failures and keeping alive the aims of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, despite the rising tide of populism and disinformation.
Guterres must step down at the end of his second five-year term on 31 December and the choice of his successor will be one of the top concerns among the scores of heads of government meeting in New York this week for the UN general assembly.
Many of Guterres’s most likely successors have shown less enthusiasm for tackling the climate crisis, despite rising alarm at its impacts, and experts have told the Guardian that some of the candidates could be “disastrous” yet could enjoy the support of influential countries including the US and its allies.

Numerous insiders and experts told the Guardian that Grossi was “trying to be a friend of Donald Trump” and maintained close links with Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, a climate denier. “Grossi is not a climate denier himself, but those links could lead him to downplay climate,” said one close observer, who could not be named.
Sall is seen as a potential champion of gas in Africa as a “transitional fuel”, which many African leaders want to exploit. “I wonder how far he would be willing to push [climate action] when it conflicts with African [fossil fuel] energy interests,” said the observer.

Huge El Niño projected to cause 450,000 deaths in next six months


New report predicts a heavy toll from Nigeria to the US – and comes on top of existing impacts of the climate crisis




More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño in the next six months, according to estimates by climate scientists.
The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, from Indonesia to India, and Nigeria to the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring.

The heat deaths have been estimated at regional level, and the researchers said the projections therefore identified where measures to protect people could be put in place and save lives. Such actions could include better heat forecasts, cooling centres where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.

The El Niño currently heating up the planet burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon on Monday, several months before its expected peak. The heat is so much greater than previous events that scientists have called it “mind-blowing” and “Godzilla-level”. El Niños are natural climate events but may be made worse by global heating.
“The estimate of 451,000 people is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” said Prof Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and at the University of Chicago, who co-authored the report.

For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.
In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025).

His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace.


Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. For one last time, António Guterres tried to fix the world’s gaze upon the dangerously escalating climate crisis. But the departing UN secretary general found world leaders still largely focused on other issues, even after a painful summer of stunning climate-driven disasters.
Speaking to assembled dignitaries at the UN on Tuesday, Guterres railed against big oil for treating “the atmosphere as an open sewer” and warned again of the catastrophic effects of the climate crisis.

What is El Niño and how is it measured?




El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared.

The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people, including those in tropical areas, has been highlighted by new research that finds they will be among the last to feel the benefits if global greenhouse gas emissions are cut to net zero.
Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to their historic range than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America.








‘Negligent’ to talk about long term risks to Australia without examining cost of climate crisis, experts say

Read more
A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan.
The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless.
The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product.


“If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero.

In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ángel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks.
This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire.
"It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years.
The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered.
It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned.
"For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later."
Wildfires
For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires.














"If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering – 'and what if we're next?'."
Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies.
World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were 40 times more likely to happen due to the warming climate.
"The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto Rodríguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association.
The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis.
"The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of Almería where a wildfire claimed 15 lives.

This year’s El Niño is already breaking records months before reaching peak intensity, with the world’s oceans recording 100 consecutive days of unprecedented heat.
El Niño, a natural warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns globally, is already the third-most intense event on record, according to a new analysis. 
The temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific reached 3.05C on 19 September, the highest daily reading in 150 years of modern measurements, according to Climate Reanalyzer, using data from the world’s top meteorological agencies. That exceeded the previous high of 3.02C in November 2015 and arrived two months earlier in the calendar year than that previous peak.





The figure is measured against the average sea surface temperature between 1991 and 2020. Another measure, ONI, which uses a rolling 30-year average and accounts for human-caused global warming, shows the event sits just a hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics draw on data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Averaged over August, the most recent full month for which data was available, the Niño 3.4 anomaly – a specific point in the Pacific used as a reference for the event as a whole – stood at 2.45C. That’s higher than every previous El Niño on record except the 2015-16 event, which peaked at 2.75C, and a reconstructed 1877-78 event which reached 2.7C based on sparse historical ship data.

El Niño events are classed as “weak” when the Niño 3.4 anomaly reaches 0.5C, “moderate” above 1C, “strong” above 1.5C, and “very strong” above 2.0C, climate scientist Zeke Hausfather explained. “For this year’s event, the Niño 3.4 anomaly has now reached 3.07C, which puts it in a statistical tie with the record set on 18 November 2015, set during a ‘very strong’ El Nino event.”


Averaging 14 seasonal forecast models, Mr Hausfather noted in Carbon Brief, the ongoing event was projected to peak at around 4.1C later this year, about 1.3C above the 2015-16 record.
Each of the 674 individual model runs in the latest analysis predicted a new record would be set. No forecasting system had previously been tested against an El Niño of this scale, he said, because none had occurred.



“The current El Niño event, which has been underway since June and is expected to last until next year, has been developing faster than any previous event on record,” Mr Hausfather wrote.

Sunshine and wind met 80.4% of demand on Australia’s main power grid on Saturday, setting a new high bar for renewable electricity.
Solar panels on rooftops provided more than half of the power used in the national electricity market, the grid that supplies the eastern states, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory, for 30 minutes around lunchtime. This was complemented by solar and windfarms, and a small amount of hydro (1%). Fossil fuels, coal and gas, contributed 20%.








Australia’s renewables transition is well under way – but meeting its 2030 target will be ‘extremely challenging’

The energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the milestone meant there was “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before”.
“There’s a long way to go, but expect more and more of these milestones in the future as Labor gets on with the job of the energy transition, and delivering real cost of living relief,” he posted on social media.

Dr Dylan McConnell, an energy systems researcher at the University of New South Wales, described it as “record season” for renewables. Clear sunny days created good conditions for generating power, coinciding with low demand from heating and cooling. It was often the time when a year’s worth of new generation coming on stream was reflected in higher shares of renewable energy.


“These records are probably not going to last very long, they’re probably going to be broken in the next couple of weeks.”
There was more renewable energy than needed. Some of the excess was being stored by pumped hydro and batteries, and quite a lot of the surplus was curtailed, due to system security rules, network constraints and low prices. Coal generation in Queensland also hit a record low over the weekend, McConnell said.
While the renewables record was a sign of progress and illustrated that Australia was “marching towards a higher penetration renewable energy system”, it was not the main game in terms of emissions, he said.
“From an emissions perspective, what matters is the annual contributions and how much coal we are burning.”

California is bracing for a record breaking El Niño that is expected to bring severe winter storms and flooding across the state, with the state’s governor declaring a state of emergency in anticipation of extreme weather in the months ahead.
The global climate phenomenon known as a “super El Niño” is already breaking temperature records and drawing predictions of an extremely wet winter in places such as California, where El Niño typically brings more severe winter storms and flooding risks. The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months ahead of its expected peak.
The latest data shows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.

The preferred measure of most meteorologists uses a 30-year rolling average as a reference and so takes account of human-caused global heating. This metric, called ONI (Nino3.4), is on the brink of breaking the record, just one-hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics are underpinned by data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).


View image in fullscreen
Damaged beachfront homes in Dana Point, California. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images
The most recent forecasts predict a peak of 4.0C in November and December, according to the average of 14 different models assessed by climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. That is a level so far above previous events that Hausfather called it “mind-blowing”, while others have described it as “Godzilla-level”. Any temperature rise above 0.5C is deemed an El Niño; above 2C is called a super El Niño.


The current El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere in which temperatures are already rising rapidly due to human-caused global heating. This double whammy means 2027 is set to “blow apart” previous records and become the hottest year ever recorded.
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.


View image in fullscreen
The Panamanian-flagged LPG tanker G. SPIRIT on the Panama Canal. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images


“Very strong El Niño events like those in 1997/1998 and 2015/2016 were associated with hundreds of billions of dollars in damages globally - this event is leaving those past ones in the dust,” said Hausfather, whose is a contributor to Carbon Brief.
Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, said: “This event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system.
“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” she said. “El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.”

Tomorrow at the United Nations in New York, the telegenic Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a tyro in international power politics, will have his first encounter in-person with US President Donald Trump, the biggest bully on the block. Will he flinch or stand his ground?



Unlike the Kennedy-Khurshev summit which unfolded over two days, Burnham has a scheduled 30 minutes, the diplomatic equivalent of a speed-date. But first impressions matter. Trump respects tough guys like China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin. Lesser mortals and smaller countries, not so much.



Burnham thinks the best way to tackle Trump is “to be yourself”. As he told football pundit and podcaster Gary Lineker: “Where you disagree, do it. But do it in a way where you’re kind of meeting where he’s at.”



Right.

Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis.
The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease.

The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria.


View image in fullscreen
A buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) on Marlborough Downs in Wiltshire, England. Photograph: Nick Upton/Alamy
The world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added.


The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans.
Aria is the brainchild of Dominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”.
The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversial geoengineering techniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer money to US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude.
One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly on Britain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. Another project developed by Rothamsted Research, the 180-year-old agricultural research facility in Hertfordshire, will edit the genes of long-lived tree species such as oaks to reproduce in months rather than decades, meaning they can rapidly develop adaptive responses to drought and invasive pathogens.

European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their great-grandparents if climate action does not ramp up quickly, a study has found.
Global heating under current policies will expose a child born in Europe in 2025 to three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather over their lifetime than someone born in 1950, the researchers found.

The number of days with the most severe conditions for fires to burn hotter and spread further will rise fastest in the Mediterranean, where generation Beta, the demographic cohort born from 2025, is to face five more years of lifetime exposure to extreme fire weather than boomers, born in the two decades after the second world war.

Read more
The hot, dry and windy conditions that let small fires explode into raging infernos have been exacerbated by one-and-a-half centuries of fossil fuel pollution and the widespread destruction of nature, which has heated the planet by 1.4C. In Europe, which has warmed twice as fast as the global average, the worsening weather has increasingly fuelled monster infernos that overwhelm authorities.
Rosa Pietroiusti, a climate researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel and lead author of the study, said severe fire weather was a “necessary but not sufficient condition” for the kind of extreme fires that ravaged parts of Europe this summer. “The meteorological conditions are an important element of fire risk – the possibility of that fire happening, being super-destructive and difficult to control, and spreading very fast.”
The researchers combined demographic data with outputs from global climate models and tallied the number of days when fire weather was more severe than the worst 5% of days for that region in the reference period from 1985 to 2014. They considered 21 scenarios that resulted in 1.5C to 3.5C of global heating by the end of the century, a spectrum that roughly covers the best- and worst-case scenarios humanity is likely to face.

How Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reports


Guardian investigation reveals fossil fuel links of IPCC authors, with experts declaring the body’s conflict of interest policy ‘not fit for purpose’




On her first day as an expert author on the world’s most important climate reports, Prof Julia Steinberger knew nobody else, so she sat down at a stranger’s table for breakfast.
“Hi, I’m Julia. I’m from the University of Lausanne,” she said. The man across the table replied: “I’m Mustafa Babiker. I work with Saudi Aramco.”

Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, is responsible for more of the carbon emissions driving the escalating climate crisis than any other company in history, and the kingdom has long been a major blocker of climate action.
Wasn’t that a conflict of interest, Steinberger asked. The UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), on which they both now sat, produces the reports that underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. No, Steinberger recalls Babiker saying: he had declared the relationship on the IPCC’s conflict of interest form. “That didn’t seem to me a very good answer, but he was friendly and we had a very nice breakfast.”


Dr Babiker has worked for Aramco for 20 years. His appointment as a coordinating lead author for the IPCC’s coming Seventh Assessment Report sparked controversy in the climate science community last year. But a Guardian investigation, carried out in partnership with a team of international journalists, has now revealed that Babiker is far from an isolated case.
At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed by or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests, the investigation found. One IPCC vice-chair, part of the body’s leadership group, also represents the kingdom at global climate negotiations as a government employee.


View image in fullscreen
Saudi Aramco’s Ras Tanura oil refinery and oil terminal. Photograph: Ahmed Jadallah/Reuters


The IPCC is the world’s most authoritative organisation on climate science, with its reports approved by 195 countries. They are produced by hundreds of lead authors from around the world with expertise ranging from atmospheric physics to the impacts of extreme weather.
The Guardian examined the 223 lead authors in working group III, the part of the IPCC that assesses how emissions can be reduced or removed from the atmosphere. Its work evaluates emissions-cutting policies and technologies and so is directly relevant to the economic interests of countries and companies. In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it?

Steve Bloomfield






As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking





If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.
The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.



All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.
Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gather for the annual summit.
The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.
It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.
Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rose in last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.


Ten years ago, the election of António Guterres of Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of the South Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.

Environmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal rule




The EPA allowed pesticide giant Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, newly released internal agency documents show.
The documents provide an unusually clear look into the process of developing pesticide regulations, which is typically done out of public view. It shows in detail how the EPA asked Bayer which regulations it wanted, received a response from Bayer, then put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule.

Dicamba is drift prone and kills vegetation and crops for miles around fields where it is sprayed, and is linked to liver cancer and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Courts have twice ordered it off the market because of its drift problems, but the EPA has re-approved it.

‘Do you have to be dead?’: US coalminers plead for benefits as black-lung disease cases surge


Trump says he digs coal – but pneumoconiosis cases are at a 50-year high, and sick miners are mired in benefit delays




For 38 years, Josh Armes worked as a coal miner in West Virginia and Virginia.
After retirement, Armes, 74, of Grundy, Virginia, was diagnosed with black lung disease, medically known as coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (CWP), caused by breathing in coal dust over long periods, which irreversibly damages the lungs.

Armes has required an oxygen tank to breathe for the pastfour years or so, along with regular doctor visits and an albuterol inhaler to help when he has trouble breathing. Even with the supplemental oxygen, he’s severely limited in what he can physically do.
In 2014, Armes received notice that the federal black lung benefits he had been receiving for more than three years were being appealed against by a coal operator. For the last 12 years, he and his family have been in an appeals process limbo, trying to regain their benefits while Armes’s condition progresses.
The federal black lung program was created in 1969 to provide coal miners disabled by black lung with monetary compensation and medical benefits. But the Armes family is just one of many who have struggled with appeals and long delays in obtaining federal black lung benefits.

Those delays come as the Trump administration moves to boost the coal industry and as cases of black lung are surging – reaching a nearly 50-year high, according to data published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine last month.


According to a May report by the government accountability office (GAO), 7,709 miner beneficiaries were receiving black lung benefits in 2024. The report was requested in 2023 by Democratic senators Mark Warner, John Hickenlooper, Tim Kaine, and John Fetterman, who have also introduced legislation to improve the black-lung benefits system.
In the fiscal year 2025, about 22,500 beneficiaries, including dependents, survivors, and miners, were receiving black lung benefits.
Between 2013 to 2024, 40% of approved claims by the Department of Labor were disputed, generally by coal operators.
The May report said miners have expressed problems with obtaining black-lung benefits. It said miners have been forced to wait several years for their claims to be approved, and raised issues with coal operators filing appeals.
“I can’t figure out one thing. They sent me a paper that said I got first- and second-stage black lung. That ought to be enough, or do you have to be dead?” Armes said.

The accelerating climate crisis and this year’s record-breaking El Niño mean that, although the summer’s heatwaves are still fresh in the memory, households in the UK are already being told to prepare for a potentially destructive winter of storms and heavy rain – leaving millions of homes at risk of flooding.
Government action is needed to improve flood defences and build reliance on a national and regional level. But with the UK’s flood season just weeks away, the Guardian spoke to experts to find out what action communities and individuals can take to make their neighbourhoods and homes more resilient, from self-closing airbricks to deflated children’s footballs.

Community action
The first step is to check whether your home or neighbourhood is listed at risk of flooding on the government’s website. If it is, find out if the local council has a flood alert scheme and make sure you and your neighbours are signed up to that and the Environment Agency’s flood alerts system.
Join any local community flood group – or consider setting one up with neighbours – and approach the council to see what flood plans it has in place, and get involved in making them better. This could include lobbying for more permeable surfaces, rain gardens and tree planting.


Identify any vulnerable residents who might need extra support and draw up a street or neighbourhood flood plan to make sure everyone knows what to do in the event of a flood.
Tracey Garrett, the chief executive of the National Flood Forum, said flooding can be “incredibly frightening and disruptive” but insists that together, communities, households and councils can make difference to an area’s resilience.
“We are seeing increasingly intense rainfall and a growing risk from surface water flooding, and climate change means we cannot assume that the flooding patterns of the past will necessarily be the patterns of the future,” she said. “This makes preparation more important than ever.”
Gardens and outdoor spaces
According to Mary Long-Dhonau, who runs the Flood Mary campaign, protecting your home starts outside. She says now is an ideal time to check brickwork and mortar on outside walls for cracks or weaknesses. These should either be repaired or replaced and external walls can be treated with a breathable waterproof sealant.

It was, according to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the “summer of truth”. Climate chaos ripped through Europe and the northern hemisphere, sending heat records tumbling, scorching crops in the fields, burning forests, emptying rivers and reservoirs, warping train tracks, melting roads and killing about 35,000 people in Europe alone.
The EU has estimated the damage at about €180bn, and the full bill is yet to arrive: harvests have been depleted, which will probably raise food price inflation, and expensive repairs to infrastructure have only just begun.

Solar panels don’t currently occupy ‘thousands of square miles’ of UK farmland




At Reform UK’s party conference earlier this month, the party’s chair Lee Anderson MP said in a Q&A session: “What we don’t want to see on farmers’ land is solar panels up and down the country. There’s literally thousands of square miles on farmland.”




This figure is not correct, and in fact it’s a substantial overstatement. Most land used for solar farms was previously agricultural land, but the total area of land estimated to be covered by them is much less than “thousands of square miles”.








In September 2024, ground-mounted solar panels covered “an estimated 21,200 hectares (52,000 acres)” or “around 0.1 per cent of the total land area of the UK”, according to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ).




21,200 hectares is equivalent to approximately 81.9 square miles, or about 0.1% of the total UK land area of 24,438,000 hectares.




The DESNZ told Full Fact this remains its latest estimate.




Last year researchers at Lancaster University produced a slightly lower estimate of up to 17,364 hectares, or 67 square miles. They estimated that of this, around 10,118 hectares (39 square miles) may have previously been arable or horticulture land.




We contacted Mr Anderson for comment.




The amount of land used for solar is expected to increase in the coming years. The government’s UK Solar Roadmap sets out that “up to 0.4% of total UK land” could be required for solar by 2030, while other projections put potential land use as even higher. But even the largest future estimates we’ve seen are less than the “thousands of square miles” referred to by Mr Anderson.













London’s white population has not ‘plummeted to 34%’




Posts shared on social media have claimed that the white population in London has dropped to 34%. But that isn’t correct, according to the latest census data.




That data, which was recorded in 2021, shows that at the time 53.8%, not 34%, of people in London identified as white.









This includes 36.8% who identified as “White: English, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish or British”, plus a further 17% recorded as “White: Other”, which includes those who said they were white Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, Roma or any other white background.




We’ve not found any more recent data reliably recording the ethnicity of London’s population, and no other credible evidence to support the 34% claim.

Australia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cards

Adam Morton






Credits are treated as a straight alternative to emissions cuts, but carbon stored in nature is different to burning millennia-old fossil fuels





The fight within the Greens that led senators to cross the floor last week over koala protection in a national park may have finally put a spotlight on a bigger issue – one at the heart of much of Australia’s promise to act on the climate crisis. It’s this: the country and its polluting industries are too reliant on carbon offsets. The more reliance is placed on them, the more they look like a house of cards.
Offsets can be a mind-deadening subject, but they matter. In Australia, they are known as Australian Carbon Credit Units. Each credit is said to represent one tonne of greenhouse gas that isn’t in the atmosphere and otherwise would have been. They are mostly generated from government-sanctioned projects that are meant to regenerate forests or capture and burn methane released from landfill sites.

These type of projects have plenty to recommend them. With global heating moving into increasingly dangerous territory, the world needs to retain and regenerate all the forests it can, and create new ones. It also needs to sharply reduce how much methane and carbon dioxide is poured into the atmosphere.
But we need to be realistic about what these carbon credits can and can’t do.
Australian carbon credits are treated as a like-for-like alternative for emissions cuts by fossil fuel producers, factories and other big polluting sites. Under the climate policy applied to big industrial facilities responsible for about a third of national pollution – the safeguard mechanism – there is no requirement that businesses make direct emissions cuts. They can just buy an unlimited number of offsets and claim them as their own reductions.


This flexibility makes life easier for the owners of industrial sites that, under changes introduced by Labor three years ago, need to cut emissions intensity – the amount of pollution pumped out per unit of production – by between 1% and 4.9% a year. But it also creates problems.
Geologically stored carbon that is dug up and used as coal, gas or oil has been underground for millennia. When it is brought to the surface and set on fire it releases heat-trapping gas that otherwise couldn’t escape. That gas can persist in the atmosphere for thousands of years.
